title: Bhishma waits for the sun
hook: a warrior on a bed of arrows waits for the sun to turn north; why families save good beginnings for after Sankranti
carry: uttarayana: the sun's bright half, when good things begin

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raksha Bandhan, and the king named in the thread's prayer. Your line was a rakhi binds a promise you keep.

The great war of the Mahabharata, and the oldest warrior on the field goes down. Bhishma, great-uncle to both sides, is struck by so many arrows that when he falls, he never touches the ground. He lies on them like a bed. And Bhishma has a gift, a boon from long ago: he can choose the moment he dies. The pain is enormous. The war goes on around him. Everyone expects him to let go. He doesn't. He looks up at the sky and says he'll wait. For the sun.
screen: `THE OLDEST WARRIOR FALLS.` → `A BED OF ARROWS.` → `HE WAITS FOR THE SUN.`

segments.voice: For weeks Bhishma lies there, and he doesn't waste the time. The family comes to him, and he teaches them about duty, kingship and God. Then the sun turns north, and only then does he let go. Why wait? Because the sun's northward half of the year, uttarayana, is held to be the bright, auspicious half: the best time to begin things, and a blessed time to leave the world. The day many Hindus mark that turn is Makar Sankranti. Sankranti means crossing: the sun crossing into Makara, the sign called Capricorn. Most festivals follow the moon, so their dates wander. This one follows the sun, so it lands in mid-January almost every year. Here's the teaching. For Hindus, time isn't all the same. Some times are shubh, auspicious, good for beginning, and families look up a muhurat, an auspicious moment, for a wedding, a new house, a first day. In many North Indian families, weddings pause in the month before Sankranti and start again once the sun has turned. And in Gujarat, whole cities climb onto their rooftops that day and fill the sky with kites. The old texts don't mention kites; the rooftops do. Some say they're thanks sent up toward the sun. And today: when your family waits for a good date, it isn't just superstition. It's the idea Bhishma held on for. What you begin, begin in the light.
screen: `BHISHMA WAITS FOR THE TURN.` · `UTTARAYANA: THE BRIGHT HALF.` · `SANKRANTI: THE SUN CROSSES.` · `SHUBH MUHURAT: A GOOD MOMENT.` · then, large: `BEGIN IN THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit where there's daylight if you can, or picture winter sun on your face. Think of one thing you'd like to begin: a habit, a conversation, a piece of work. Don't start it yet. Just hold it, the way Bhishma held on, and choose a moment to begin it, a morning, a day, on purpose. If you pray, offer it to the sun with folded hands, the way many Hindus greet Surya at dawn. Then breathe out slowly.
Makar Sankranti. The day the sun crosses into Makara and turns north, the start of the bright half of the year.
Your line: uttarayana, the sun's bright half, when good things begin. Bhishma waited for it. Day one hundred fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: On Makar Sankranti, in mid-January, many Hindus bathe in rivers, give to those in need, share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Gujarat and elsewhere spend the day flying kites from rooftops to mark the sun's turn north into uttarayana, the auspicious half of the year when many families plan weddings and new beginnings.

notes: Uttarayana: the tradition dates it from Makar Sankranti; astronomically the northward turn begins at the December solstice, and the sidereal date has drifted with precession. The script says 'what the tradition calls'. A Keeper may want the drift mentioned or not.
Bhishma's wait: roughly 58 nights in some counts; written as 'for weeks'. Confirm.
Explanations for kites are presented as 'people give different answers'; 'the texts don't mention kites' — confirm no classical source prescribes kite flying.
Ahmedabad setting; paper lanterns (tukkal) at night. Confirm.
